match.reason: The closest bank point, River health in the basin, covers water taken for farms and towns harming wetlands, but it is broader (salinity, algal blooms, dams) and never says irrigation uses most of Australia's water or links the harm to dry years, so it teaches a different scope.

draft.title: Farming and water use
card: Irrigation means watering crops and pasture with water taken from rivers, dams or underground. Farms need it where rain is too low or too uneven to grow crops.
Irrigated farming uses most of the water that Australia takes from its rivers. Cotton, rice, dairy pasture and orchards are common irrigated farm types.
Water taken for farms is no longer in the river. In dry years, when river flows are already low, this can leave too little for wetlands and wildlife.
Wetlands, fish and river red gums depend on river water. Less flow can dry out wetlands and harm the animals and plants that live there.
draft.remember: Farms take most of the river water Australia uses, and in dry years the rivers and wetlands can be left short.

a.q: Why can irrigated farming harm wetlands in a dry year?
opts: Water taken for farms leaves less river flow to reach them
Irrigation adds extra water that floods the wetlands
Wetlands need dry conditions, which irrigation removes
Farms stop rain from falling over the wetlands
a.why: River flow is already low in a dry year, and water taken for farms is no longer in the river. Less flow reaches wetlands. Irrigation does not add water to a river, so flooding is the wrong cause.
a.clue: Think about where irrigation water comes from.

b.q: Dev grows rice on an irrigated farm beside a river in southern New South Wales. In a drought he takes his usual amount of river water. What is the most likely effect downstream?
opts: Less water reaches downstream wetlands and wildlife
Downstream wetlands get more water than usual
River flow downstream is not affected at all
Downstream wildlife gains from the extra rain
b.why: Water Dev takes is removed from the river, so less flows on downstream. In a drought the river is already low, so wetlands and wildlife feel the loss most. Taking water cannot leave flow unchanged.
b.clue: Water taken out of a river cannot flow on downstream.

a.best: Water taken for farms leaves less river flow to reach them

b.best: Less water reaches downstream wetlands and wildlife

problems.detail: The clue 'Water taken out of a river cannot flow on downstream' all but states the right answer, so a student can pick it without applying the idea.

check.summary: Facts and answers check out. The only problem is that question b's clue nearly gives the answer away.
